item.title: White House turns hit song against Noah Kahan after singer fumes over Trump manufacturing post
item.description: The White House mocked Noah Kahan with a Trump Derangement Syndrome jab after the singer objected to "American Cars" being used in a Trump post.
item.content:encoded:
The White House hit back at folk-pop singer Noah Kahan on Thursday, after the artist expressed outrage over the Trump administration using his track "American Cars" to highlight American manufacturing.

The Grammy-nominated singer criticized a joint Instagram post from the White House and the official POTUS account featuring President Donald Trump touring a General Motors test facility in Michigan with the caption "Made in America is BACK."

The use of the song "American Cars" led users online to tag the singer, who responded directly in the comment section.

Kahan wrote Tuesday on Instagram, "Would never approve of my music being used in support of you or this administration." Levine, a co-writer on the song, responded with profanity, according to Variety, writing, "You fat f---, this song isn’t for you."

JOURNEY STAR JONATHAN CAIN DEMANDS BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN 'SHUT UP,' ACT LIKE HE WAS BORN IN THE USA

Rather than backing down, the White House mocked the singer's criticism, as first reported by The Hollywood Reporter. Kaelan Dorr of the White House Office of Digital Strategy took to X, writing, "Symptoms of TDS apparently include having a northern attitude." Instagram has since listed the post’s audio as "unavailable."

"TDS," short for Trump Derangement Syndrome, is a term frequently used by conservatives to describe hostility towards the president. The X post also referenced Kahan’s hit song "Northern Attitude," which has racked up over 700 million streams.

Kahan joins a growing list of musicians who have objected to the administration's use of their music on social media or at rallies, including Sabrina Carpenter, SZA, Celine Dion and Beyoncé.

POP STAR NOAH KAHAN FUMES AFTER TRUMP WHITE HOUSE USES HIT SONG 'AMERICAN CARS' FOR GM VIDEO

MEGAN MORONEY CANCELS SHOW MID-PERFORMANCE, LEAVES STAGE IN TEARS

In November 2025, Disney star turned singer Olivia Rodrigo called out the White House and the Department of Homeland Security for using her song in a post encouraging illegal immigrants to self-deport. She took to Instagram to express her outrage, writing, "Don’t ever use my songs to promote your racist, hateful propaganda."

A DHS spokesperson told Fox News Digital earlier this year, "America is grateful all the time for our federal law enforcement officers who keep us safe," referencing Rodrigo's "grateful all the time" lyric. "We suggest Ms. Rodrigo thank them for their service, not belittle their sacrifice."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Most recently, Katy Perry condemned the White House’s use of her song "Firework" over footage of military strikes, writing that she "did not approve this" and does not condone its use.

Kahan has largely stayed out of national political battles, choosing instead to focus on advocacy for mental health resources.

He founded the "Busyhead Project," whose website describes it as a "non-profit mental health organization" which "aims to end the stigma around mental health and improve access to resources.

" In recognition of his efforts, Vermont Republican Gov. Phil Scott declared Sept. 19 "Noah Kahan's Busyhead Project Day."

item.title: Ja'Marr Chase throws helmet as fight breaks out on first day of Bengals training camp
item.description: Ja'Marr Chase launched a helmet and jawed with the entire defense during a heated Cincinnati Bengals training camp practice with cornerbacks DJ Turner and Jalen Davis.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals began their training camp on Wednesday, and fuses were lit almost immediately.

All-Pro receiver Ja'Marr Chase found himself in the middle of quite the brouhaha during practice, launching a helmet in the process.

It's not clear what started the ruckus between Chase and cornerbacks DJ Turner and Jalen Davis, but Chase "jawed with the entire defense," according to WLWT.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

The Athletic also reported that a punch was thrown, but it's not known by who.

Davis later told reporters that the skirmish was nothing more than "just competing."

"That's all it is," he said.

In fact, he even said he wanted there to be a fight "every day."

"I always feel like the energy's gotta be like that. It's gotta be like that on both sides of the field," Davis added.

BEARS LEGEND BRIAN URLACHER TALKS TEAM'S LIKELY MOVE, USC SON'S COLLEGE CAREER

Davis even squared up at Chase for a split second before cooler heads prevailed.

The Bengals defense hasn't shown much fight in recent years, giving up the third-most points in the NFL last season and the seventh-most the year prior.

Chase was named a First-team All-Pro for the second time in as many years this past season, cementing himself as maybe the game's best receiver. In his first five seasons, he has eclipsed 6,837 yards on 767 receptions and 54 touchdowns - an average of 113 catches, 1,490 yards and 11.8 scores per season.

Cincinnati went 6-11 last year and lost Joe Burrow to a severe case of turf toe.

This brief fight wasn't the only news out of Cincinnati, as defensive lineman Shemar Stewart suffered an ugly-looking leg injury and had to be carted off.

item.title: Hunter Biden reveals he's 'definitely not running' for office despite media tour
item.description: Hunter Biden told the "Macrodosing" podcast hosts he's "definitely not running for anything" despite his many recent public appearances and buzz.
item.content:encoded:
Former President Joe Biden's son, Hunter Biden, said during an interview on Wednesday that he wasn't running for office, despite his many recent public appearances.

Barstool Sports' "Macrodosing" podcast host, known as Big Tennessee, said, "As I see you making the rounds, it just seems like a guy who might want to run for something. And then I saw you come in the building today."

The host said his introductions as he entered the building were "of somebody that wants to run."

JOE AND HUNTER BIDEN APPEAR ON BARSTOOL PODCAST TO PRESENT ‘LIB OF THE YEAR’ AWARD

"I'm definitely not running for anything," Biden said, joking that if he secured the Barstool host's endorsement he might.

"Those were the introductions of a politician," the host added.

The former president's son has made numerous appearances on podcasts in the last few months.

KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY

Biden has appeared on NPR's "Newsmakers," and the podcasts of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Don Lemon and "I've Had It," as well as those of far-right figures.

Newsom joked during Hunter's interview on his show that he was a 2028 presidential candidate, and said the ex-president's son had a lot of buzz.

The former president's son also fiercely defended his father during the "Macrodosing" podcast, and attributed then-President Biden's weak 2024 debate performance to having cancer.

JILL BIDEN SAYS SHE THOUGHT JOE WAS HAVING A STROKE DURING HIS DISASTROUS 2024 DEBATE PERFORMANCE

"My dad walked out and he literally, for the first time in my life, I’ve ever seen this, he looked like a deer in the headlights. He looked blank. And what do I attribute that to?… I mean, we didn’t find out until nine months later that he not only had stage four prostate cancer, but he had stage four metastatic bone cancer, which means that it had been metastasizing for over a three-year period of time," he said.

Biden's cancer diagnosis was not revealed until last year.

Hunter Biden said during the interview that his father's debate appearance was a complete surprise to him, and said he hadn't seen him like that until that night.

Biden also claimed he hadn't seen his father like that since. Shortly before he left office, President Biden pardoned his son in late 2024 ahead of his sentencing for tax evasion and federal gun charges.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Hunter Biden also told the hosts of the "I've Had It" podcast in July that his father's greatest mistake was appointing Merrick Garland to be his attorney general.

"My take is this, and removing myself from it as much as I can, my personal feelings, is the single greatest mistake of my father's administration was the leadership of Merrick Garland," Hunter Biden said.

Fox News' Lindsay Kornick contributed to this report.

item.title: War powers resolution fails as Senate Republicans stand by Trump on Iran
item.description: Senate Republicans blocked another war powers resolution as munitions dwindle and Sen. Bill Cassidy draws a hardline on ground troops in Iran.
item.content:encoded:
Despite reports of waning munitions, spiking gas prices and concerns of no clear objectives moving forward, Senate Republicans are still giving President Donald Trump wiggle room in the war in Iran.

Republicans again blocked another war powers resolution to force an immediate withdrawal of America’s military might from Iran on Thursday. Senate Democrats have tried and failed to convince enough of their Republican colleagues to consistently buck the war over a dozen times as it stretches into its fifth month.

The latest effort from Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., failed along similar lines as last week’s effort, where only a small cohort of Senate Republicans crossed the aisle to end the war.

REPUBLICANS FALL IN LINE WITH TRUMP ON IRAN WAR DESPITE RISING COSTS AND US DEATH TOLL

One Republican who did join Democrats, but has since reversed course, is Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., who got into a shouting match with Trump and demanded a briefing on the situation in Iran.

He got that briefing and has since flipped his vote, which he acknowledged was used as "leverage to get some information." Still, he doesn’t totally support what’s going on, but used "All the King's Men" as an example to show that the situation and the politics of it are not black and white.

"It is a gradation," Cassidy said. "What we're doing here is a gradation, a murkiness, a vagueness, but we're trying to see our way through it. And I'm trying to see my way through it."

WATCH: SCHUMER'S ANTI-CORRUPTION SPEECH DERAILED AFTER HECKLER BRANDS HIM 'GENOCIDAL MANIAC'

But he drew a hardline on ground troops entering Iran.

"If there are ground troops, by definition, there needs to be a declaration of war from Congress on this, period," Cassidy said.

The latest votes come as reports of munitions continuing to dwindle have reverberated through Congress, and as the Pentagon and War Secretary Pete Hegseth plead for more defense funding.

HEGSETH DISMISSES ‘FOOLISH’ US STOCKPILE CONCERNS AS IRAN CONFLICT TESTS MUNITIONS

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who has been wary of the war but has so far not broken with Trump to back Democrats’ resolutions, said, "Obviously, it’s concerning" that the nation’s munitions stockpile is dropping, but countered that a closed-door debriefing on the matter could sate concerns.

"And of course, if they are chronically low and affecting war strategy, then we should make it a priority," Tillis said.

When asked whether he had been adequately briefed, Tillis said, "No."

Munitions have been a concern throughout the war in Iran, and with renewed strikes starting last week, they are again back at the forefront of the conversation about the strategy in the region.

A report released Monday from the Center for Strategic and International Studies found, for example, that renewed fighting in the Middle East found that Patriot and THAAD interceptor missiles, which are used to thwart incoming projectiles and drones, had dwindled from prewar inventories of 2,330 and 452, respectively, to 759 and 234 missiles.

"I think there's pretty solid information that our military is short on munitions, not their fault," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said. "Trump launched this war impulsively, without a clear set of achievable objectives, and planning for how to conduct it."

"The basic failure to plan the amount of munitions that would be necessary is a fatal failing that is directly the responsibility of the commander-in-chief," he continued.

item.title: San Diego Padres favored over Giants as Robbie Ray likely makes final start before trade deadline
item.description: Robbie Ray may be making his final Giants start before the trade deadline as San Diego's Padres look to capitalize on his struggles on the road.
item.content:encoded:
It is hard to believe we are almost at August. This is where we will start seeing some separation of teams that are truly playoff contenders and those that are going to start looking at next year. We know the trade deadline is in just a few days, so that will be the first indication of who is giving up and who wants to advance. We have one team that will certainly sell - the Giants - taking on a team that might sell or might buy - the Padres.

The San Francisco Giants haven't had really anything go the way they wanted this season. Despite making some good additions and having some very good players on the roster, they just can't seem to make this team work. It is a bit crazy because the team is hitting with a .254 batting average, good for sixth in the league. They just aren't scoring many runs. They are 21st in the league at 457. Their slugging percentage is among the best in baseball, but their on-base percentage is 23rd. It just really doesn't make much sense.

Their pitching does have some issues, and they have a collective 4.36 ERA. Their bullpen struggles and is in the bottom third of the league with a 4.37 ERA. However, they've had some decent bright spots with people like today's starter Robbie Ray. Despite all the trade rumors around him, Ray is having a solid season with a 9-6 record and a 3.16 ERA and a 1.31 WHIP. He has struggled away from San Francisco with a 4.35 road ERA compared to just 2.22 at home. He hasn't faced the Padres this season, but he hasn't done great against them, either. Collectively, San Diego hitters are hitting .273 in 110 at-bats against him.

The San Diego Padres are still a winning team, but they are also frustrating because their lineup should be resulting in much better outcomes. The Padres are 55-53 overall, but with all of the names on this team, you have to think they are underperforming. Their struggles are a bit more obvious. Two of their most important pieces are having down years. Manny Machado is finally batting over .200, and Fernando Tatis Jr. has just eight homers. It also doesn't help that a guy like Xander Bogaerts is hitting only .218 as well. Injuries have been an issue, but the team hasn't hit the way they are capable of doing.

If the Padres can turn it on for the final two months, they should have most of the pieces needed to battle a team like the Dodgers. The problem is that it seems like this team will limp its way to the finish line this season. The starter for tonight's game is JP Sears, who has a 3.86 ERA and a 1.18 WHIP. Sears has only made six appearances and five starts this year, highlighting the injury issues on the team. Sears has not thrown more than five innings in a start this month, but the Padres bullpen is one of the better in the league.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

This is probably the last start that Ray will make for the Giants. I have to imagine they ship him off to a contender. Sears has looked pretty good in his few outings, but I think the team knows to get him through the opposing lineup twice and get him out of the game. I don't have a great feel for the total as I think both teams could put up runs or be stifled by their opponent. I'm taking the Padres on the run line; I think they are the better team, have the better bullpen, and Ray has struggled on the road. Give me the Padres -1.5 at +139.

(Note: The Padres are -157 on the moneyline, I try to not give out a bet higher than -140, but if you're more comfortable with just betting on the Padres winning, go for it.)

item.title: License plate cameras are tracking drivers everywhere
item.description: The DeFlock map displays about 119,000 license plate readers across the U.S., with Flock Safety cameras accounting for 83% of the mapped total.
item.content:encoded:
One minute, you are driving to the grocery store. The next, a camera above the road photographs your car and adds the sighting to a searchable database. You probably will not hear a click or see a flash. In fact, you may never notice the camera mounted on a pole near the intersection.

Automated license plate readers have quietly spread across the country. As of our reporting, the open-source DeFlock map displayed about 119,000 readers across the United States. DeFlock is a community-powered project that maps reported camera locations using public submissions and data from OpenStreetMap. Because the map relies partly on crowdsourced information, it may miss some cameras or include locations that have changed.

Flock Safety cameras account for about 83% of the mapped total. California has the largest number of mapped readers, with more than 16,000. Major clusters appear around Los Angeles and the Bay Area. Police say the cameras help locate stolen cars and vehicles connected to serious crimes.

FLOCK SURVEILLANCE SPREADS ACROSS THE SOUTH AS RED-STATE LAWMAKERS SEEK TO AX '1984'-STYLE TRACKING TOOLS

However, privacy advocates warn that the same network can reveal where ordinary people travel throughout the day. Each sighting can include a vehicle's plate number, appearance, location and the time it passed the camera. Flock says its system can search by plate, vehicle type and visible features.

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

Automated license plate readers, also known as ALPRs or LPRs, have become common tools for police departments. Businesses and homeowners associations can also install them. The rules can vary depending on who owns the camera and who gets access to the data.

The cameras often appear on poles near streets, intersections and neighborhood entrances. Some have solar panels attached to the pole. As a car passes, the camera takes a photograph. Software reads the license plate and turns the image into a searchable record. CyberGuy previously found that license plate cameras are also scanning vehicles at some Home Depot and Lowe's parking lots.

Flock Safety has become one of the largest vendors in this market. Its cameras connect to a cloud-based system where authorized customers can review vehicle sightings. Unlike red-light cameras, these readers generally focus on identifying vehicles. They typically do not issue traffic tickets. Still, every passing vehicle can enter the database. The driver does not need to face suspicion or have any connection to an investigation.

A reader begins with your license plate number. However, the record can include much more than the characters printed on the plate. The system records a vehicle's make and model. It can also note the color and body type.

Visible features may become searchable as well. These can include a roof rack, bumper sticker or missing hubcap. The record also includes the camera location and a timestamp. Together, those details show where the vehicle appeared and when it passed. Flock says its license plate reader system focuses on vehicles rather than faces. The company also says its LPR cameras exclude facial recognition and biometric identification.

A single camera sighting may reveal little about your day. Several sightings can start to form a pattern. For example, a vehicle that appears near the same house each evening may reveal where someone lives. Another record could show a visit to a medical provider.

A license plate can also connect a car to information held by a state motor vehicle agency. That connection can help investigators identify the registered owner. Authorized personnel can search for a complete plate number. They may also search using a partial plate or vehicle description.

A department looking for a dark SUV with a roof rack could receive several possible matches. Investigators would then need to confirm which vehicle they want. That search ability can save time during an urgent case. Meanwhile, it also gives agencies access to information about drivers who have done nothing wrong.

California leads the country with more than 16,000 mapped readers, according to an analysis of DeFlock data. Florida followed with 7,169 cameras. Georgia had 7,046. Illinois had 5,822. The concentration becomes clearer when the figures are compared with road mileage. San Francisco County ranked third nationwide with 1,196 cameras per 1,000 road miles. Only New York County and Kings County ranked higher.

In Southern California, Orange County ranked No. 33 nationwide. It had 184 cameras per 1,000 road miles. Los Angeles County ranked No. 59 with 143 cameras per 1,000 miles.

However, DeFlock cannot provide a complete camera inventory. The open-source project relies on public reports and data from other sources. As a result, populated communities may have more markers because more people submit camera locations. Rural areas may appear less covered even when readers exist there. A missing marker cannot guarantee that a road has no camera. Likewise, some mapped locations may need updates after a camera moves or disappears.

Police departments can place license plates connected to stolen vehicles on a hotlist. They may also add cars linked to active investigations. When a camera detects a matching plate, the system can alert officers. That may help them locate a stolen car or find a missing person's vehicle. Investigators can also search earlier sightings. Those records may show where a vehicle appeared before or after an incident. However, an automated alert still requires human verification.

A recent LAPD review examined more than 210 million plate scans over two months. The system incorrectly flagged 161 plates as stolen. Yet not every incorrect alert led to a police encounter. During the same period, 337 alerts helped officers recover stolen vehicles. Those results show both the investigative value and the risk of an incorrect match.

License plate readers collect information from millions of vehicles. Most belong to people with no connection to a crime. Privacy advocates say connected camera networks can create a detailed driving history without requiring a warrant. They also worry about access by agencies far from the community that installed the camera.

Those concerns have already affected ordinary drivers. CyberGuy reported on a Colorado woman who was wrongly accused after Flock camera records linked her truck to the area of a porch theft. She had to gather Google Location Timeline data, vehicle camera footage and other evidence to prove where she had been. Police later voided the summons and dropped the case.

California law limits how local law enforcement agencies share automated license plate reader information. The state prohibits local agencies from giving ALPR data to federal authorities or out-of-state agencies. State officials say the information must remain within California.

However, allegations of improper sharing have raised questions about whether every agency follows those restrictions. California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued the city of El Cajon in October 2025. His office accused the city of sharing ALPR data with more than 100 out-of-state law enforcement agencies.

In January 2026, Bonta asked a court to order the city to stop the sharing. The case remained part of California's effort to enforce its ALPR privacy laws. The dispute highlights a gap between written policy and technical enforcement. A rule may prohibit sharing, but the system also needs controls that block unauthorized access.

THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

The Los Angeles Police Department entered a three-year operating agreement with Flock Safety in 2023. The arrangement covered access to data from 138 pole-mounted cameras across the city. The agreement expired on July 11, 2026. LAPD allowed it to lapse while officials addressed concerns involving data ownership, privacy and security. The department also wanted clearer limits on how Flock could store, share and use information collected by the cameras.

The 138 cameras continued operating after the agreement ended. However, LAPD employees no longer had regular access to the data they collected. That information remained stored in the cloud and could become available to investigators if the city finalizes a new agreement. Police officials began negotiating proposed terms with stronger safeguards. Under those terms, the city would retain ownership of every image, record and piece of metadata captured by the cameras.

Flock would also be prohibited from selling, publishing or sharing the information with outside organizations. In addition, the company could not use the data for commercial purposes or to train artificial intelligence systems. As of our reporting, LAPD and Flock had reportedly not finalized a replacement agreement, and talks are believed to be ongoing.

LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell called the technology a valuable investigative tool. Still, he said the department needed to use it responsibly. The dispute shows how quickly a camera program can raise difficult questions about control and oversight. Those questions become harder to resolve after a large network has already begun collecting information.

Flock rejects claims that its license plate readers continuously track a vehicle. The company says each camera captures a vehicle at one specific location. However, authorized agencies can search separate sightings stored within the system.

Flock says its default retention period lasts 30 days. Customers may choose a different period based on local laws or contract terms. The company also says customers control their information and sharing settings. According to Flock, every search is connected to a specific account and recorded in an activity log.

However, access questions can become more complicated when public-records laws enter the picture. CyberGuy previously reported that a Washington judge ruled Flock license plate reader images can qualify as public records, even when a private company stores the files for a city. The decision did not mean every driver record would automatically become public. However, it showed that using an outside vendor may not remove government surveillance data from state transparency laws.

Flock also says it does not sell customer data or use facial recognition with its LPR cameras. It says automated deletion and annual security audits help confirm that agencies follow their selected retention periods. Those safeguards address part of the privacy debate. Yet their effectiveness depends on how each customer configures the system and reviews employee activity.

You may never receive a notification when a license plate camera records your vehicle. Still, you can learn more about the readers operating around your community.

Check DeFlock at deflock.org for reported cameras near your home and regular driving routes. Remember that public submissions help build the map. Therefore, it may contain gaps or outdated locations. Look for cameras mounted high on narrow poles. A nearby solar panel can also signal a roadside reader.

Search your city or police department website for its ALPR policy. The policy may explain how long the department keeps vehicle records. It should also describe the types of investigations that allow a search. Do not assume every agency uses Flock's 30-day default. Contracts and local rules can set a shorter or longer retention period.

Find out whether other departments can search your community's camera data. A city may have strict internal rules while sharing access with a much larger network. That wider access can make local safeguards harder to evaluate. Look for an agency transparency portal if one exists. You can also request a list of connected departments from your city.

City council agendas often reveal proposed camera purchases before installation begins. Search meeting documents for terms such as "ALPR," "automated license plate reader" or "Flock Safety." Contract documents may show how many cameras the city plans to install. They can also explain who will own the records. Public meetings give residents a chance to ask questions before officials approve a larger network.

Ask who reviews searches for possible abuse. Audit logs offer limited protection when nobody checks them. You should also find out what happens after an employee violates the policy. Departments should explain whether they suspend access or begin an investigation. Strong consequences can discourage personal searches. They also show whether an agency treats its privacy rules seriously.

License plate readers can help police find a stolen vehicle or develop leads after a serious crime. That explains why departments, businesses and homeowners associations continue installing them. Still, these cameras record everyday drivers who have no connection to an investigation. A series of sightings can reveal where you go and when, even though the camera never captures your face. The Colorado case shows what can happen when a camera record points police toward the wrong person. Meanwhile, the Washington ruling raises another concern because some images held for a city may qualify as public records. Flock says customers control their data and can review searches through activity logs. Those protections depend on departments limiting access, checking for misuse and enforcing their own policies. LAPD's decision to pause access after its agreement expired shows that privacy concerns can slow a major camera program. However, the ongoing talks suggest the technology will remain part of the public safety debate. Before more cameras appear, your community deserves clear answers about who can search the records, how long the data stays available and what happens when someone abuses access.

Would you accept license plate cameras throughout your community if police said they helped solve crimes, or has this type of tracking already gone too far? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: Florida AG threatens Fauci investigation after Senate hearing
item.description: James Uthmeier says his office is launching a Florida investigation into Anthony Fauci after the former NIAID director invoked the Fifth Amendment.
item.content:encoded:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said he will be opening up an investigation into Dr. Anthony Fauci, former National Institutes of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) director, following Fauci's explosive decision to invoke his Fifth Amendment right and not answer any questions during a congressional hearing Wednesday.

"Fauci's lack of candor to Congress is unbelievable. My office is launching an investigation into Dr. Fauci. It's past time we get the truth of what happened during COVID," Uthmeier wrote in a Wednesday post on X.

Uthmeier expanded on his decision in an exclusive statement to Fox News Digital.

FAUCI PLEADS FIFTH WITH 'ZERO LEGAL JUSTIFICATION' AS CRITICS ERUPT AND DEMAND CONTEMPT CHARGES

"In light of recent reports exposed by Senator Rand Paul, we will investigate any and all potential violations of Florida law involving Anthony Fauci," Uthmeier told Fox News Digital.

"Our inquiry will focus on what Fauci knew, when he knew it, and how he misled the American people. We will examine the physical and monetary harms to Floridians that may have resulted from his deceptions and determine whether his conduct exposes him to liability under state law," Uthmeier's statement concluded.

Uthmeier cited revelations published by Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., which revealed internal notes Fauci wrote on government computers during his time at NIAID.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

The internal notes, which Paul and others have taken to referring to as Fauci's "diary," suggest Fauci appeared to publicly overstate the death rate from COVID-19 compared to what he wrote privately.

"[Former CDC Director] Tom Frieden called me this AM and we discussed various aspects of the outbreak," Fauci wrote on Feb. 8, 2020.

"He and I are on the same page in thinking tht [sic] this is acting like a bad influenza in its transmissibility and that the denominator is much greater than 34,867 (above) making the case fatality rate (CFR) more like 0.2-0.3 % rather than 2.0%," Fauci's entry concluded.

However, a month later, in congressional testimony to the House Oversight Committee on March 11, 2020, Fauci pegged the mortality rate at 1%.

"I think if you count all the cases of minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic infection, that probably brings the mortality rate down to somewhere around 1%, which means it is 10 times more lethal than the seasonal flu," he testified.

When called to testify on the revelations before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Wednesday, Fauci exercised his Fifth Amendment right and refused to answer legislators' questions 111 times.

Uthmeier is not the only Republican to take aim at the former COVID czar in light of the revelations.

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Wednesday that Fauci should be held in congressional contempt for refusing to answer questions despite receiving a presidential pardon.

"I think Anthony Fauci has had contempt for Congress and contempt for the American people for decades," he said. "His diary shows that he deliberately lied to the American people over and over and over again."

Paul, for his part, said his committee will vote on whether to hold Fauci in contempt next week.

item.title: Online fury erupts as conservatives recall ’insane’ COVID-19 lockdown policies after Fauci takes the Fifth
item.description: Anthony Fauci pleaded the Fifth 111 times at a Senate hearing as conservatives resurfaced viral videos of COVID lockdown arrests and mask mandates.

item.content:encoded:

Point Dume is situated entirely within Census tract 8004.08, which the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey estimated was just 0.2% Black and roughly 94% White as of 2019.

Harris's choice of neighborhood may surprise longtime observers given past comments she has made about the importance of living among other Black Americans.

"It was more, for me, about the numerosity than it was the diversity, I grew up in a community where there were many representations of diversity," she added. "Going to Howard, there were so many (Black people)! And they’re all in your age group, in your phase of life."

As a presidential candidate, she proposed $100 billion in assistance for families in historically redlined communities and as vice president she promoted the Biden administration’s efforts to combat racial bias in home appraisals.

item.title: 'Hot seat rankings' for all 16 SEC coaches as beginning of 2026 college football season draws nearer
item.description: Shane Beamer's South Carolina seat is radioactive heading into 2026, while Kalen DeBoer and Josh Heupel face rising expectations at their programs.
item.content:encoded:
At the beginning of every college football season, there are always a few questions that are on every fan's mind.

One of which is "who looks like they can win it all every season," but since I already addressed that earlier this week, I'm here to tackle the second most popular question: which coaches are on the hot seat heading into fall?

More specifically, I wanted to look at every coach from the SEC and give them a "hot seat ranking" based on their job security in 2026.

PERCEPTION IS REALITY, AND THE SEC NEEDS TO START WINNING AGAIN BEFORE IT CONTINUES TO PUFF OUT ITS CHEST

I will be lumping all 16 SEC coaches into one of five categories that should give everyone an idea of where these guys stand before the start of the season.

We have a lot to get to, so let's get this hot seat party started.

The SEC has six "new" coaches among its ranks in 2026, and the reason I put a heavy set of quotations around that word is because some of these guys have already been coaches in the conference.

Obviously, Lane Kiffin was previously at Ole Miss for six years and even had an infamous stop in Knoxville for one season to coach the Tennessee Vols, but if we want to get technical, the Rebels have a "returning" SEC coach of their own in Pete Golding.

The colorful successor to Kiffin in Oxford guided Ole Miss to the College Football Playoff semifinals in 2025, but 2026 will be his first full season, so I'm including him here.

None of these guys are getting fired in their first season, so they earned themselves a ranking almost completely removed from the rest of the guys on this list.

THREE SEC WIN TOTALS YOU SHOULD ABSOLUTELY POUNCE ON BEFORE THE 2026 COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON BEGINS

Sure, if Kiffin has a first-year implosion and finishes 6-6, he will certainly be sitting on a blazing hot seat coming into 2027, but no one else is even close to that talk right now.

Enjoy it, men. Odds are you will never feel this secure in your job again.

The seat can't get much colder than this, and ironically enough, these two coaches sit on opposite ends of the royalty spectrum in the SEC.

Kirby Smart has earned every bit of the job security he has going for him, as the Georgia Bulldogs head coach enters year 11 of his storied career in Athens.

In 2021, the man delivered a national championship 40 years in the making to a starving fanbase then followed it up with another the very next year just for good measure.

Though Georgia fans aren't thrilled with their recent lack of CFP success, the Dawgs are still reigning SEC champs and look like the favorites to win the league again in 2026, so Kirby's seat is ice cold.

For Clark Lea, just the fact that he had Vandy of all programs knocking on the door of the Playoff last season means his seat couldn't get any colder.

For crying out loud, the man won ten games at Vanderbilt, something no coach has ever done in program history.

When you couple that with the fact that guys like Diego Pavia, Eli Stowers, and a smattering of offensive linemen aren't in Nashville anymore, fans rightly expect the Commodores to take a step back in '26, cooling the seat even more for Lea.

Vandy could go 2-10 this year and I still don't think Clark Lea will be packing his bags. Now THAT'S job security.

These three coaches are sitting on some pretty cool seats, all things considered.

While the situations aren't perfect, they can't get much better for at least two of the three names in this category.

Mike Elko led the Texas A&M Aggies to an 11-win season and a Playoff berth, and for a fanbase desperate to shed those pre-World War II championship taunts, it feels like a step in the right direction.

When you pair the winning with A&M's historic recruiting class that is brewing for 2027, Elko is as cool as a cucumber.

The same goes for Eli Drinkwitz, who experienced a bit of a step back in 2025, but still won eight games and has things trending up in Columbia.

Drinkwitz earned a massive extension after being courted by a few big boy job openings like Florida and Penn State, and while that doesn't always guarantee job security (as I'll explain later), it is a nice bonus to help keep the seat cool.

Steve Sarkisian is the outlier here, as I almost put him in the next category.

I don't believe Sark is in any danger of losing his job, hence the cool seat, but the expectations for this season are so high that, should he fail to deliver, we could be having an entirely different conversation 365 days from now.

But that hasn't happened yet, so for now, Sark and Texas are rolling and 2025 should be considered just a minor blip on the radar.

Things start warming up in this category; perhaps these coaches are starting to sweat through their team-issued polos.

No coach in this category is in any immediate danger of being fired during the 2026 season, but a bad start could really raise those temperatures in a hurry.

For three of the four coaches here, it's all about expectations.

DeBoer, Heupel, and Venables have all been solid to very good throughout most of their tenures at their respective schools.

The problem is that all three are at programs that demand excellence.

DeBoer in particular is standing in the shadow of perhaps the biggest giant to ever coach in the Southeastern Conference, and although he just signed an extension to stay in Tuscaloosa, having an empty trophy case with regard to SEC and national championships is starting to make the natives very restless.

Another season without a deep Playoff run could send DeBoer packing.

Heupel's rope is a touch longer than Venables', given that this year is supposed to be a ramp-up for what should be a loaded 2027 roster in Knoxville, but the Vols have zero Playoff wins entering year six of his tenure.

Finally, Jeff Lebby probably deserves to be in the tier above this one, especially since the Bulldogs were a barren wasteland of talent when he came to town and they were a few plays away from potentially being an eight or nine-win team last year.

But another sub-.500 season will almost certainly give even the most patient fans and boosters in Starkville a reason to start looking for the exit door of the Lebby era.

I wrote an article last month about how you could make the argument that Shane Beamer's seat is the hottest in the country, and that includes a man by the name of Mike Norvell.

Beamer's seat is radioactive heading into the 2026 season, and much of that has to do with that dirty word, "expectations," again.

South Carolina was a dark-horse candidate to make the College Football Playoff last season and ended up face-planting to the tune of a 4-8 campaign.

A similar 4-8 season for a CFP hopeful in Florida cost Billy Napier his job, so another subpar record in 2026 could spell doom for Beamer and co.

The Gamecocks have an incendiary talent at quarterback in LaNorris Sellers, a freak athlete at wide receiver in Nyck Harbor, and an all-conference selection and future first-round draft pick at edge rusher in Dylan Stewart, so the pieces are in place, at least in theory, to have a good bounce-back year.

Anything less than 8-4 is probably a massive disappointment in Columbia, and I could honestly see Beamer being shown the door if South Carolina isn't at least 4-2 by the time their bye week rolls around.

The SEC is a cutthroat league, and Beamer could end up being the latest casualty before the season is even over.

item.title: Travelers clash after TSA shares surprising guidance about airport etiquette
item.description: In a playful post, the TSA recommended travelers consider bringing a hammock to the airport to relax while they wait. Some flyers felt it was a genius hack; others said it was ridiculous.
item.content:encoded:
The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) has sparked debate about airport etiquette after recommending that travelers bring hammocks to airports so they can relax during long layovers.

In a recent post marking National Hammock Day, the agency wrote, "Nobody said you couldn't bring a hammock to the airport."

It added, "To reduce tension, or to avoid having a falling out with the airport, check with them about where you can and can't hang your napping apparatus."

FLIGHT ATTENDANTS BEG TRAVELERS TO STOP DOING THE ONE THING THAT ANNOYS CREWS MOST

The post included photos of travelers relaxing in hammocks strung up inside airport terminals.

July 22 marked "National Hammock Day, so we highlighted the occasion on our social media channels," the TSA told Fox News Digital. 

Diane Gottsman, an etiquette expert based in San Antonio and founder of The Protocol School of Texas, said most travelers understand that delays and layovers can be exhausting — but that doesn't mean personal comfort should come at the expense of others.

"Bringing your own hammock through security for the specific reason of setting up camp is not considerate of others in a tight public space," Gottsman told Fox News Digital.

She noted that each airport has its own rules and safety policies.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Before you get caught stringing up your suspended apparatus between two poles, ask airport staff if there is a safe, out-of-the-way place to hang within the rules of the airport," Gottsman said.

Permission to use hammocks inside terminals usually depends on individual airport rules and applicable local rules. 

She said most travelers will likely continue choosing an uncomfortable airport chair over turning a terminal into a campsite. 

The post sparked debate online, with some social media users arguing that airports have become too casual.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

"Airports used to be a civilized place," one user wrote on X.

Others pointed out that the TSA only determines what passengers can bring through security checkpoints.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"TSA doesn't control the airport," one Reddit user wrote. "Every airport will have its own rules."

Others argued that hanging a hammock inside an airport could create safety concerns or obstruct other travelers.

"I love my hammock, but this would be obnoxious," one Reddit user wrote.

Some travelers, however, fully embraced the idea.

"I vowed to myself to always travel with my hammock," one Reddit user wrote after describing using one during a long layover before eventually being asked by airport police to take it down.

item.description: OPM's new rule removes 1978 hiring guidelines tied to disparate impact, marking a deeper push to dismantle the legal framework behind federal DEI policies.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration on Wednesday took another step in its sweeping campaign to eliminate DEI policies from the federal government, removing decades-old hiring guidelines that officials say encouraged race-conscious employment decisions in favor of a renewed emphasis on merit-based hiring.

The U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) issued a final interim rule on Thursday that removes references to the 1978 Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, which govern employee selection standards, citing a recent Justice Department legal opinion that found the guidelines unconstitutional in the way they encouraged race-conscious decision-making.

The move affects how federal agencies approach hiring by eliminating references to long-standing guidance centered on "disparate impact," the idea that hiring practices that could produce unequal outcomes among racial groups can be legally problematic even absent intentional discrimination.

Administration officials argue those guidelines pressured employers to focus on racial outcomes rather than qualifications, while supporters of the guidelines contend they help guard against subtle forms of discrimination.

DEI HIRING BOOST FOR ONE BLUE STATE'S MUSLIM COMMISSION INITIATIVE FLIES IN FACE OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WOKE PUSH

"Federal hiring should be based on merit, qualifications, and the ability to perform the job," OPM Director Scott Kupor said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"This rule ensures OPM's regulations reflect legal guidance while preserving the rigorous, job-related standards that help agencies recruit and hire the most qualified workforce in service to the American people."

The rule took effect immediately after it was published in the Federal Register on Thursday but will remain open for public comment for 60 days before OPM decides whether to make it permanent.

COAST GUARD ENDING RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS FOR OFFICER COMMISSIONING PROGRAM UNDER TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN

OPM serves as the federal government's human resources agency, setting hiring, personnel and workforce policies for roughly 2 million civilian federal employees across executive branch agencies. It oversees the rules governing how federal agencies recruit, hire, promote and manage their workforces.

This move serves as the latest example of the administration moving beyond simply shutting down DEI offices or ending diversity training and now targeting the legal and regulatory framework that critics argue enabled DEI policies in the first place.

KEY TRUMP AGENCY PUTS TOP UNIVERSITIES IN CROSSHAIRS OVER ALLEGED RACE-BASED DORM PROGRAMS

Since the beginning of President Donald Trump's second term, the administration has highlighted hundreds of colleges that have rolled back DEI initiatives, along with policy changes involving transgender athletic participation, parental rights, race-conscious programs and merit-based admissions.

They also dismantled federal DEI programs, terminated DEI-related grants and contracts, cut ties with companies embracing DEI policies, required federal contractors to comply with the administration's requirements, and warned schools they could lose federal funding over certain DEI practices.

item.title: Trump threatens to yank his own AG nominee as GOP revolt grows
item.description: Trump threatened to withdraw Todd Blanche's nomination until John Cornyn and Thom Tillis leave office, escalating a standoff over his tax settlement.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump is taking a hardball tactic against Republican rebels demanding concessions for their vote to confirm Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche.

After Blanche’s confirmation hearing was postponed late Wednesday night, Trump took to Truth Social Thursday morning to excoriate the two key holdouts on the Senate Judiciary Committee standing in the way of his personal lawyer becoming the nation’s top prosecutor: Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C.

Trump threatened to withdraw Blanche’s nomination until both are out of office next year.

TRUMP AG PICK BLANCHE STALLED AS KEY REPUBLICANS REFUSE TO BUDGE

"Todd Blanche is a STAR, and everyone knows it! He has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time," Trump said. "However, John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting."

"Remember, both Cornyn and Tillis voted for Merrick Garland, and others, too numerous to mention," he continued. "I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office."

DEMS REJECT TRUMP’S TOP SPY PICK AFTER DEMANDING REPLACEMENT, LEAVING COUNTER-TERROR TOOL IN AIR

While Trump did thwart Cornyn’s re-election bid by backing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton as the Republican nominee, Tillis opted to retire on his own volition last year after raging over Trump's "big, beautiful bill."

Cornyn shrugged off the threat almost immediately. Both he and Tillis are in pursuit of explicit, written proposals to modify the settlement deal reached between the IRS and Trump and his family earlier this year.

"POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis," Cornyn said on X.

DOZEN GOP REBELS FAIL TO PERMANENTLY KILL TRUMP'S CONTROVERSIAL $2B FUND

Their resistance and demands caused Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, to postpone Blanche’s confirmation hearing scheduled for Thursday morning. Without their support, he wouldn’t be able to make it to the Senate floor.

Negotiations are still ongoing, but so far, the duo have not gotten specifically what they want to permanently kill the now-defunct, nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund and a rewrite of Trump’s audit immunity baked into the settlement deal.

Meanwhile, there’s no guarantee that the Senate would be more accepting of Blanche next year, either, given that Republicans have more seats in danger than Senate Democrats.

Trump could leave Blanche as acting attorney general for some time, similar to how former President Joe Biden left former acting Labor Secretary Julie Su in the role from 2023 to the end of his presidency.

item.title: Ex-Dem operative details 'new donor establishment' behind Mamdani-era progressives: 'Not from the grassroots'
item.description: A former progressive fundraiser reveals how dark money super PACs and DSA candidates are reshaping the Democratic Party after its 2024 electoral loss.
item.content:encoded:
Evan Barker, a former Democratic operative turned voter for President Donald Trump, detailed alleged dark money influence that she says has driven the party further left.

Barker, who raised money for Democratic candidates throughout her career, from Barack Obama to progressive lawmakers such as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., before deciding to vote for Trump in 2024, explained in an interview with Fox News Digital that the party's major shift influenced her decision to defect.

"I first got activated in Democratic politics when Barack Obama was running in 2008. And if you look at him then and you compare him to the modern movement of the party today, it is just night and day. They have gone left on so many critical issues, like immigration and identity politics and defund the police and just all of these things that I did not sign up for," she told Fox News Digital.

HOW THE 'LONG MARCH' THROUGH THE INSTITUTIONS LED TO SOCIALIST TAKEOVER OF DEM PARTY: 'NEED TO WAKE UP'

She argued that the party, in her eyes, abandoned the working class and ignored Americans like her family in Kansas.

"It was also seeing the way the people that I knew in progressive politics looked at people in the middle of the country. People like my family who had voted for Obama and then voted for Donald Trump, and they really just had a disdain for them. They truly did view them as deplorables. And then it got even worse when I saw them actually decide to write them off. To say that they would not even try to persuade them to vote for us anymore because there was no point," she told Fox News Digital.

"At that point, I knew the party was doomed, and I think I just experienced so much abuse working in the movement that at some point I got fed up and I was like, 'I'm gonna do this, like what other options have they given me?'" Barker added.

JAMES CARVILLE ARGUES ONE KEY MISTAKE FROM BIDEN HAS LEFT DEMOCRATS IN DISARRAY

In her new book, "Nothing Left: Confessions of a Democratic Operative," Barker writes about her trepidation and hesitance to vote for Kamala Harris after the party chose her to replace President Joe Biden as the Democrats' presidential candidate in 2024.

"I would say that Kamala Harris was me seeing in real time the manifestation of everything the Democrats had become. They were a party that was loud but said very little. They were a party without substance. They were empty. They were hollow," she told Fox News Digital.

"When I went to the DNC, I only saw Kamala talk about abortion and shouting out joy," Barker recalled. "She wasn't focused on the southern border, she wasn't focused on the economy. She wasn't connecting to the pain that people like my mom were experiencing in Missouri and it just became too much. And when they had Oprah Winfrey out to speak to tell us all that we should be feeling joy and to ignore everything that we were feeling, I had enough and I left. I left the convention before she even spoke."

MAMDANI CALLS OUT DEMOCRATIC PARTY AS 'WELL-PAID CONSULTANTS AND BIG MONEY INTERESTS'

Barker was on site for one of the first meetings between Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and then-House candidate Ocasio-Cortez in 2018, when the pair flew to Kansas to stump for Brent Welder, a progressive House candidate who Barker was fundraising for at the time, she explains in her book.

While at the time Barker felt that Ocasio-Cortez could and should run for president, she now feels that the progressive congresswoman and other members of the "Squad" represent everything that's wrong with the party.

"I think AOC in 2018 and the 'Squad' members that came out of her rise have actually done the most damage to the Democratic Party," she told Fox News Digital.

"I actually think that Bernie Sanders ran a very different campaign in 2015 and 2016 than how he is today. I think back then he was more moderate on issues like immigration. He was more moderate on guns, he wasn't anti-gun, you know, he didn't really talk about identity politics. And I think with the rise of AOC, she was identity-obsessed. And so was Ilhan Omar, and so was Jamaal Bowman," Barker continued.

As a fundraiser for the Progressive Change Campaign Committee (PCCC) and Left Rising, Barker said she raised money for progressive candidates. Barker argued the party's production of far-left stars like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani shows that Democrats are learning the wrong lessons from their 2024 losses.

"There was a brief period of time after the 2024 election when I really thought that maybe Democrats would learn lessons — losing multiple times to Donald Trump. I mean, come on. Like, what more do they need to wake them up? And instead, I just saw them go further to the left, with Zohran Mamdani, AOC, and all these DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] candidates that kind of have sprung up over the last cycle," she told Fox News Digital.

She attributed the DSA and other progressives' rise to the groups' alleged newfound willingness to deal in dark money.

"The biggest difference between then and now, and part of the reason we just saw somebody like Darializa Chevalier win in New York, is because the progressives, the DSA, they have learned how to utilize outside, independent expenditure, dark money super PACs to their benefit. They used to be afraid to go there because it contradicted with their principles, but after 10 years they've wised up and they've actually started playing the same games as the establishment and in many ways have created the new donor establishment in the Democratic Party, and I think that's what many people don't realize," Barker told Fox News Digital.

A spokesperson for Chevalier denied the charge that she takes corporate PAC money in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Darializa does not take corporate PAC money, AIPAC money, ICE money, or money from people looking to harm or push people out of this community. She is accountable only to the people of this district. That’s a win for every tenant, every immigrant, and every working person in this district who deserves a representative who actually answers to working class people instead of corporate donors, CEOs, or lobbies. Our campaign was not only the first challenger candidate in NY-13 history to pass the $1 million raised mark, but Darializa also raised that staggering sum as a first-time, working class candidate from more than 10,000 individual donors and with an average donation of just $66," the statement read.

Dark money and donors, Barker claimed, play a much larger role in progressive politics than most voters know.

"Most of the messaging is crafted by heads of organizations, consultants and especially donors," she told Fox News Digital.

"You know, I talk about one donor in my book, Leah Hunt-Hendrix, an oil heiress from Texas, and she ran a big donor network and at the same time was interfacing on campaigns and working with candidates. And they have a lot of influence over what candidates talk about, you know. It's hard to say no to someone who knows so many wealthy people and can connect to so many different people when they're giving you advice on what policies to adopt and how to speak about policy," she continued.

"I would say the majority of the ideas in the Democratic Party are not from the grassroots. But ironically, and this is kind of interesting, I think a lot of the base now at this point has been radicalized, so they are not necessarily disagreeing with what the Democratic elites are pushing," Barker added.

She explained the anatomy of a progressive pet policy and how the preferred party lines work their way from donors down to voters.

"It's a combination of donors and consultants and the heads of organizations that push candidates into adopting their policy positions. When I was working with the far-left, around the year of 2020, something that I saw that was extremely worrisome to me actually was that any organization — it didn't matter if they were a veterans organization, just focused on veterans issues, or if they were a healthcare organization, just trying to focus on healthcare — donors demanded the concept of intersectionality to bring to all messaging related to these issues," she told Fox News Digital

"So that meant that if you were talking about veterans issues, you also had to be talking about racial justice or environmental justice or criminal reform justice. So they kind of pushed all of these other very unpopular, far-left social issues and moved them into the economic issues as well in a way that completely eroded their trust with the public and pushed people like me further away from them," Barker concluded.

Fox News Digital contacted the Democratic Socialists of America, Ocasio-Cortez, Mamdani, Chevalier, Sanders, Omar, Bowman and Hunt-Hendrix, via her Way to Win organization, for further comment.

item.title: US Navy plans major torpedo stockpile overhaul as military shifts to two-war strategy
item.description: The Navy's torpedo overhaul targets MK-48 and MK-54 production as lawmakers push a two-war strategy amid depleted missile stockpiles from the Iran war.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Navy is poised to overhaul its torpedo inventory under the newly-approved congressional budget as the military shifts toward a "two-war" strategy.

Lawmakers made it clear that the U.S. needs to build quantities of undersea weapons sufficient to maintain two major regional conflicts simultaneously, according to Naval News.

Manufacturers are now focused on building up supplies of the U.S. MK-48 Advanced Capability (ADCAP) heavyweight torpedoes and MK-54 lightweight torpedoes to meet the minimum base requirements set by the new budget.

US DRAINS CRITICAL MISSILE STOCKPILES IN IRAN WAR AS YEARSLONG REBUILD LOOMS

The Navy has not clarified the exact number of undersea weapons that would entail, but it is based on internal estimates about potential conflicts with a near-peer forces.

The Navy is also required to build up a plan to massively increase torpedo production should it become necessary during war or peacetime.

The overhaul comes as the U.S. military is already scrambling to refill stockpiles of missiles and other weapons depleted in the war against Iran.

HEGSETH DISMISSES ‘FOOLISH’ US STOCKPILE CONCERNS AS IRAN CONFLICT TESTS MUNITIONS

Defending Israel and the Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar from Iranian counterstrikes during the recent 12-day exchange of strikes cost the U.S. and Israel between $1.48 billion to $1.58 billion, according to an analysis by the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA).

The monthslong conflict has burned through a significant number of America's offensive and defensive missile systems.

The U.S. had roughly 632 Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors before June 13, the day Israel began its offensive in Iran. About 540 interceptors remain in its arsenal based on JINSA’s calculations of interceptor deliveries and use, according to the report.

THE TWO MOST IMPORTANT AMERICAN WEAPONS SYSTEMS NATO IS EAGER TO HAVE

The U.S. has used up 14% of its global stockpile of prized THAAD missile interceptors. America’s THAAD system accounted for nearly half of all interceptions due to the "insufficient" capacity of Israel’s Arrow interception system. 

It would take three to eight years to replenish the THAAD interceptors used in the 12-day war at current production rates.

Patriot interceptor production is more robust than THAAD, according to the report, but the U.S. is providing a number of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine. So, it’s unclear how many remain in the stockpile.

Fox News' Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

item.title: New York City immigrant business owners are planning to sue Mamdani over taxpayer-funded supermarkets
item.description: The Multicultural Business Coalition voted to sue New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his taxpayer-funded grocery stores plan that threatens small businesses.
item.content:encoded:
Several immigrant business owners are preparing to sue New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his plan for city-owned grocery stores, Fox News Digital confirmed on Wednesday.

The New York Post first reported on Tuesday that the Multicultural Business Coalition’s (MBC) board voted to file a lawsuit against the city over Mamdani's plan to open five taxpayer-funded grocery stores that will sell food at prices up to 30% below traditional retailers.

According to MBC Chairman Frank Garcia, the MBC is now planning to send a letter to Mamdani's office in the coming days detailing its upcoming legal plans to protect competing stores, bodegas and other small businesses. If Mamdani does not respond or meet with the organization within the next three weeks, the group plans to take further legal action.

MAMDANI CONFRONTED ON FAILED CITY-RUN GROCERY STORE ATTEMPT IN KANSAS CITY, CLAIMS HIS PLAN WILL WORK

"The [New York City] commissioner said this administration is open to speak to everybody, and they want to hear from everybody," Garcia said to Fox News Digital. "So I've been waiting for a meeting for a couple of months. Why aren't they having me?"

He added, "We are ready to file the lawsuit if the mayor doesn't meet with us."

Garcia also emphasized that the lawsuit is a nonpartisan initiative and is primarily focused on raising awareness for small business owners struggling with rising costs in New York City. Though the lawsuit has not yet been filed, he said that his lawyers will be "ready to go" after the three-week deadline thanks to broad support from other organizations.

STEPHEN A SMITH SLAMS MAMDANI'S POLICIES, SAYS HIS BIGGEST FANS 'ARE NOT PEOPLE WHO PAY BILLS EVERY DAY'

"We're nonpartisan. So we're going to meet everybody, Republican or Democrat. There was a Democratic Jewish organization. There were others that we're gonna meet with [along with] civil rights organizations. We're gonna be with all the different civil rights organizations that are willing to support this and have the funding already to fund this," Garcia said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the mayor's office for comment.

The MBC, which was founded earlier this year to oppose Mamdani's grocery store initiative, is composed of members from African, Asian, Caribbean, Hispanic, Jewish and Middle Eastern business communities. The organization has also received widespread support from city and state lawmakers such as New York State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins.

NYC MAYOR MAMDANI CALLS THREAT OF RICH PEOPLE LEAVING NYC OVER TAXES 'IMAGINED'

The announcement of a lawsuit came after Mamdani unveiled more details about his city-backed grocery stores, which faced renewed criticism as a "communist fantasy."

Mamdani also faces a lawsuit from New York City landlords hoping to overturn the city's rent freeze.

item.title: Fauci haunted by 2022 'nothing to hide' vow after invoking the Fifth Amendment 111 times
item.description: A resurfaced 2022 CNN interview clip shows Dr. Anthony Fauci saying he had "nothing to hide" from Congress, but he invoked the Fifth Amendment 111 times at his hearing.
item.content:encoded:
Dr. Anthony Fauci’s words are coming back to haunt him after resurfaced comments from a 2022 interview with CNN showed a complete 180 on his attitude toward testifying before Congress.

"I am very happy to testify before any congressional oversight committee," Fauci told CNN in 2022.

Fauci, under his lawyers’ guidance, did not answer a single question from Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., or others on the committee about his COVID-19 pandemic response or gain-of-function research, instead invoking the Fifth Amendment 111 times.

SEN RAND PAUL QUESTIONS WHETHER FAUCI'S INVOKING THE FIFTH AMENDMENT WAS VALID AFTER BIDEN PARDON

"I have nothing to hide. I can explain and validate everything that I’ve done… I’m going to do what I need to do, and that is cooperate fully, because we have nothing to hide at all," he added in the CNN interview roughly four years ago.

Fox News Digital reached out to Fauci for comment on his 2022 assertion. 

Fauci argued during Wednesday’s hearing that Paul, who recently released more than 1,000 pages of his personal diary entries, has an "obvious obsession" with pushing for his prosecution.

He said the diary release was designed to "get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, quote, behind bars, unquote."

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

"Although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government, and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions," Fauci told the Senate committee before invoking the Fifth Amendment 111 times.

Meanwhile, Rand Paul, who has spearheaded the investigation of Fauci, is looking to challenge whether the COVID leader was legally justified in pleading the Fifth Amendment, given that he is a recipient of a presidential pardon.

"The legal question is, if you're pardoned, can you really claim the Fifth?" he said on "The Will Cain Show" on Wednesday. "The Fifth Amendment is to claim immunity from self-incrimination. But if you've already been given immunity, you can't self-incriminate unless you lie."

Paul is seeking a vote to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress after the former public health official pleaded the Fifth 111 times at Wednesday’s contentious congressional hearing.
